title: Paper Money
objective: After this level you can explain how paper money began in China and spread around the world.
summary: Paper money began in China: Tang merchants' flying money, then Song-era notes in Sichuan, where iron coins were heavy. Europe's first banknotes came from Sweden in 1661.

cards.headline: Paper money was invented because coins were too heavy. Literally.
cards.body: In 11th-century China, and again in 17th-century Sweden, people's coins were so heavy that a paper promise was simply easier to carry.

cards.headline: Flying money
cards.body: It started with merchants in Tang dynasty China (618–907). Rather than haul heavy coins on long journeys, they used paper drafts nicknamed "flying money". Was that the first paper money? The British Museum says yes; other historians call it a draft for moving funds, more like a money order than cash. Either way, paper had started standing in for metal.

cards.headline: Sichuan's iron problem
cards.body: In 11th-century Sichuan, people used iron coins, which were heavy. So they left their coins on deposit and carried paper certificates instead, which could be spent in their place. Around 1023, the Song government took over issuing them. These notes, called jiaozi, are widely described as the world's first paper currency.

cards.fact: Europe's first real banknotes came from Sweden in 1661.
cards.context: Marco Polo had described China's paper money back in the 13th century. Then Stockholms Banco issued notes, and they caught on for a familiar reason: Sweden's copper coins were heavy and cumbersome. But paper is only a promise. When the public lost confidence in the bank, it failed. Why people trust paper at all is Level 6's question.

cards.headline: Paper money: printed
learned: Heavy iron coins pushed Sichuan to paper

questions.prompt: People in 11th-century Sichuan switched to paper certificates because _____.

options.label: iron was needed for weapons
options.rationale: The problem was carrying the coins, not a shortage of iron.

options.label: the emperor banned all coins
options.rationale: Coins stayed on deposit; the paper stood in for them.

options.label: paper was worth more than iron
options.rationale: The paper's value came from the coins it stood for.

questions.explanation: Iron coins were heavy, so people deposited them and spent paper certificates instead.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in paper money's story in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Tang merchants used flying money (618 to 907), the Song government took over jiaozi around 1023, Marco Polo described China's paper money in the 13th century, and Stockholms Banco issued notes in 1661.

questions.prompt: Level 4 praised metal as money. What drawback of metal coins did paper fix, in both Sichuan and Sweden?

options.label: Metal coins rotted over time
options.rationale: Metal doesn't perish; that's one reason it made good money.

options.label: Metal coins were too easy to fake
Heavy coins were a pain to carry
Metal coins had no stamp
options.rationale: Coins had stamps from the very start in Lydia.

questions.explanation: Iron in Sichuan and copper in Sweden were heavy and cumbersome. Paper carried the same value in your pocket.
